content.intro: This lesson studies Exploring a Vue Project within Vue Project Structure and Application Basics. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding the project skeleton makes it easier to find the right file and diagnose setup or build errors instead of changing unrelated parts.

content_blocks.title: Exploring a Vue Project: URL-driven navigation
content_blocks.alt_text: URL-driven navigation diagram for lesson 9: Exploring a Vue Project. Represent addressable navigation in the route → Resolve route parameters and navigation policy → Render the matching route component
content_blocks.caption: Routing flow: the URL determines the matched view; frontend guards improve navigation but do not secure backend APIs.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: A Vue project combines Single-File Components, an application entry point, Vite tooling, assets, and package configuration. This lesson focuses on Exploring a Vue Project. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: src , public , and project configuration
items.text: For src , public , and project configuration, trace the path from the entry point to the root component, then identify the configuration or tool responsible for compiling and serving it. Use the official create-vue/Vite workflow for a fresh Vue 3 project and keep dependency versions reproducible.

items.title: The main.js entry point
items.text: For The main.js entry point, trace the path from the entry point to the root component, then identify the configuration or tool responsible for compiling and serving it. Use the official create-vue/Vite workflow for a fresh Vue 3 project and keep dependency versions reproducible.

items.title: The root App.vue component
items.text: For The root App.vue component, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Assets and reusable components
items.text: For Assets and reusable components, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Views, routes, and application entry points
items.text: For Views, routes, and application entry points, keep the URL as the addressable navigation state, use named route records when practical, and handle invalid parameters or failed navigation explicitly. A route guard improves navigation flow but does not replace backend access control.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Exploring a Vue Project with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “The main.js entry point”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: A Vue project combines Single-File Components, an application entry point, Vite tooling, assets, and package configuration. For Exploring a Vue Project, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Exploring a Vue Project” that applies “src , public , and project configuration”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “src , public , and project configuration”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
